item.title: You can’t blame NZ PM Luxon or PM Rabuka for crimes – Singh
item.description: Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh has questioned whether Prime Ministers of New Zealand Christopher Luxon and Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka should be blamed for individual crimes occurring in their respective countries, as he responded to concerns about vandalism and damage to places of worship. Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Singh referred to recent break-ins involving t
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh has questioned whether Prime Ministers of New Zealand Christopher Luxon and Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka should be blamed for individual crimes occurring in their respective countries, as he responded to concerns about vandalism and damage to places of worship.

Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Singh referred to recent break-ins involving two of his friends in Epsom, Auckland, to argue that individual incidents should not automatically be attributed to a government or its leader.

“Last week in New Zealand I had two friends, two friends whose house was broken into, in Epsom,” Mr Singh said.

“Epsom is a high-class area of Auckland. Now, do you then blame Mr Luxon, the Prime Minister, because of what had happened?”

“Do you then blame Honourable Rabuka here?” Mr Singh asked.

Mr Singh went on to criticise the former government, claiming problems facing the country had developed over its 16 years in office.

Speaker Filimone Jitoko subsequently intervened and directed the Minister back to the question.

“You’ve done enough background analysis,” the Speaker said.

Addressing the substantive issue, Mr Singh said his Ministry strongly condemned vandalism, damage or deterioration of any place of worship.

“This Ministry strongly condemns any act of vandalism, damage or deterioration of places of worship, whether it involves Hindu temples, churches, mosques or any other places of religious significance,” he said.

Mr Singh said such acts were contrary to the values of religious tolerance, respect and peaceful coexistence.

He said the Ministry had visited a number of affected sites and engaged directly with communities.

Mr Singh said circumstances differed between incidents, with some appearing isolated while others had raised concerns among affected communities over whether they could have been religiously motivated.

He also noted that many places of worship, particularly temples, were easily accessible to the public and had limited security or caretaker presence outside worship hours.

item.title: Children as young as 10 trapped in drug addiction
item.description: Children as young as 10 to 14 years old are becoming trapped in drug addiction in Fiji, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week. Ms Kiran said decades of exposure to illicit drugs had left families vulnerable, despite efforts by national taskforces to disrupt drug supply chains.
item.content:encoded:
Children as young as 10 to 14 years old are becoming trapped in drug addiction in Fiji, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week.

Ms Kiran said decades of exposure to illicit drugs had left families vulnerable, despite efforts by national taskforces to disrupt drug supply chains.

“Most concerning of all, children as young as 10 years to 14 years of age are now becoming trapped in the cycle of addiction,” she said.

“These figures are not merely statistics — they reflect a profound national challenge that demands coordinated, compassionate and evidence-based intervention.”

Ms Kiran said police records traced the influx of hard drugs to before 2009, with the situation continuing to worsen.

She said Fiji recorded 1501 illicit substance cases in 2020, including 100 involving methamphetamine and four involving cocaine.

“The data paints a sobering picture,” she said.

Ms Kiran said the impact was being seen through rising youth mortality, crime and public health risks, including HIV transmission through shared needles.

She said Fiji had historically lacked an integrated recovery programme specifically designed for adolescents, while a shortage of specialist child psychologists and psychiatrists had also affected treatment outcomes.

“Today, Madam Deputy Speaker, we are actively changing this narrative,” Ms Kiran said.

She said Government, in partnership with Empower Pacific, had established Fiji’s first dedicated residential recovery facility for adolescent boys aged 14 to 17.

The Lautoka facility, named Na Sala Vou — “a new pathway for our boys” — provides a structured environment for young people to recover, learn and rebuild their lives.

“This represents a monumental milestone, Madam Deputy Speaker, and a powerful statement of our belief that every child deserves a second chance, that recovery is possible, and that healing is our collective responsibility,” Ms Kiran said.

item.title: Government talks consultation but fails to deliver – Koya
item.description: Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya has accused the Government of repeatedly preaching “consultation, consultation, consultation” while failing to adequately involve the public before introducing major legislative changes. Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Koya pointed to several pieces of legislation which he claimed demonstrated shortcomings in the consultation process.
item.content:encoded:
Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya has accused the Government of repeatedly preaching “consultation, consultation, consultation” while failing to adequately involve the public before introducing major legislative changes.

Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Koya pointed to several pieces of legislation which he claimed demonstrated shortcomings in the consultation process.

“They stand here and harp about consultation, consultation, consultation. Yet they do not do it thoroughly,” Mr Koya said.

He cited the Tourism Bill, Crimes Decree and Criminal Records Bill 2025 as examples.

“The Tourism Bill was never thoroughly discussed with the people, the Crimes Decree was never thoroughly discussed with the people,” he said.

“The Criminal Records Bill 2025, we went out as a committee and when we spoke to the people, they said they were not consulted.”

Mr Koya also revisited changes to the Liquor Act, which reduced nightclub operating hours from 5am to 1am on public safety grounds.

He said while concerns about brawls, robberies and public safety were legitimate, the economic consequences for businesses should have been properly considered before the changes were introduced.

“There were businesses that were still recovering from COVID-19, but you shut them down,” Mr Koya said.

He said the Government eventually reversed course on the operating hours and claimed the experience demonstrated why meaningful consultation was important.

Mr Koya also questioned an earlier consultation cited by Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga.

“He even said when he was asked by me, where did you do the consultation? ‘We did the consultation in Levuka somewhere with respect to that’,” Mr Koya said.

Mr Koya said he was not opposed to amending laws but argued consultation should identify potential consequences before legislation was changed.

“The experience should teach the Acting Attorney-General and this Government an important lesson — the purpose of consultation is to identify these consequences before we amend the law,” he said.

“We have no problem in amending the law, but you must look at its purpose properly.”

item.title: MCF Church President Turagavou calls for end to levy system
item.description: Methodist Church in Fiji President Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou has called on the Church to move away from its traditional levy system and transition towards “heart and faith giving.” Speaking at the Church’s Annual Conference today, Rev Dr Turagavou said the change would require time, education and trust from members.
item.content:encoded:
Methodist Church in Fiji President Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou has called on the Church to move away from its traditional levy system and transition towards “heart and faith giving.”

Speaking at the Church’s Annual Conference today, Rev Dr Turagavou said the change would require time, education and trust from members.

“We should erase the mentality and practice of the levy system, and the Church should operate from the basis of heart and faith giving,” he said.

“In this regard, I call on every division and circuit, and every church to begin the transition toward heart and faith giving.”

Rev Dr Turagavou acknowledged that changing the Church’s approach to giving could not happen immediately.

“This will not happen overnight. It requires teaching. It requires trust, and requires that we, as the Church, provide our people with something worth believing in.”

He also stressed that the Church’s spiritual development and management of its financial and physical assets should go hand-in-hand.

“Our spiritual growth and the development of the resources God has entrusted to us — our wealth, our land, our properties — must never be treated as two separate journeys. They are one journey,” he said.

“A church that is spiritually alive but careless with what God has given it will fall down. A church that manages its resources wisely but has lost its spiritual heart will become an empty institution.”

Rev Dr Turagavou said the Church headquarters had been deliberately investing resources through its business arm as part of efforts to strengthen its financial position.

He pointed to the opening of its first service station and the development of a commercial complex as signs that the investments were beginning to produce returns.

“I am pleased to report this investment. It begins to bear fruit,” he said.

Rev Dr Turagavou said responsible stewardship of Church resources was important to ensuring investments generated funds that could be directed back into the Church and its mission.

item.title: Yellow card made me more popular – Minister Singh
item.description: Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh says receiving a “yellow card” in Parliament made him more popular, with people calling him to express their sympathy following the incident. Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Singh reflected light-heartedly on his temporary suspension from the House after Opposition MP Jone Usamate earlier raised a point of order.
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh says receiving a “yellow card” in Parliament made him more popular, with people calling him to express their sympathy following the incident.

Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Singh reflected light-heartedly on his temporary suspension from the House after Opposition MP Jone Usamate earlier raised a point of order.

“I must thank the honourable Usamate that he raised a Point of Order, which actually made me more popular in this country when I got a yellow card from Parliament,” Mr Singh said.

“This is the first in this session we got that, and of course, a lot of people called me and sympathised about what I had said.”

Mr Singh also responded to comments from Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu about his absence from Parliament during the week.

“I think the honourable Leader of the Opposition missed me throughout the whole week. He kept on saying that I am not around,” he said.

“Yes, I was around because I have got other business to do, apart from in Parliament.”

Mr Singh then explained why he had remained away from the chamber longer than required following the “yellow card”.

He said he had misunderstood the length of time he was required to stay out of Parliament.

“I was actually given one and a half hour, but I misheard that it [was] one and a half days, so I did not come back until the Secretariat called me to say that it was one and a half hour,” Mr Singh said.

Mr Singh’s comments followed the parliamentary disciplinary action which he referred to as receiving a “yellow card”.

item.title: Lasawa elected Methodist Church President Elect for 2027
item.description: Reverend Dr Jolami Lasawa has been elected President Elect of the Methodist Church in Fiji for 2027, following leadership elections at the Church’s Annual Conference today. His election was one of the major outcomes of Day Three of the Methodist Church in Fiji Annual Conference 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Reverend Dr Jolami Lasawa has been elected President Elect of the Methodist Church in Fiji for 2027, following leadership elections at the Church’s Annual Conference today.

His election was one of the major outcomes of Day Three of the Methodist Church in Fiji Annual Conference 2026.

Rev Dr Lasawa will assume the presidency in 2027 and provide spiritual and pastoral leadership to one of Fiji’s largest Christian denominations as it continues its mission and ministry in Fiji and abroad.

The Conference also elected current Methodist Church President Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou as General Secretary Elect for 2027.

Rev Dr Turagavou’s election will see him transition from the presidency to the senior administrative position next year.

Meanwhile, elections were also conducted for the position of Assistant General Secretary, currently held by Reverend Dr Anil Reuben.

The result is expected to be announced tomorrow.

Rev Dr Reuben’s current five-year term as Assistant General Secretary concludes in April 2027.

Apart from the leadership elections, Conference members continued deliberations on a range of issues affecting the Church and its institutions.

Matters relating to the Davuilevu Theological College, Deaconess Order and Women’s Fellowship were among those discussed.

Representatives of the institutions and departments were given opportunities to respond to questions and provide clarification on issues raised by Conference members.

The discussions form part of the Church’s efforts to strengthen theological education, ministry, fellowship and its wider institutional operations.

The Methodist Church in Fiji Annual Conference continues this week, with further deliberations and leadership announcements expected.

Attention will now turn to the remaining elections and discussions as the Church prepares for a significant leadership transition in 2027.

item.title: US visa suspension overturned
item.description: FIJIAN nationals planning to permanently migrate to the United States have received a significant boost after a US federal court struck down a policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance to citizens of Fiji and 74 other countries. The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled on Friday that the nationality-based policy was contrary to law and exceeded the statutory
item.content:encoded:
FIJIAN nationals planning to permanently migrate to the United States have received a significant boost after a US federal court struck down a policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance to citizens of Fiji and 74 other countries.

The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled on Friday that the nationality-based policy was contrary to law and exceeded the statutory authority of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The court ordered the policy vacated under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Fiji was among the 75 countries targeted under the policy introduced by the US Department of State in January.

The suspension, which took effect on January 21, was based on concerns that immigrants from the designated countries were at higher risk of using welfare or becoming a “public charge”.

Under the directive, consular officers were required to refuse immigrant visas to nationals of the listed countries even where an individual assessment found an applicant was otherwise eligible.

The court found this approach unlawful, noting US immigration law prohibits discrimination in the issuance of immigrant visas based on nationality.

The ruling is particularly significant for Fijians pursuing family-based or employment-based permanent migration to the United States.

The court ordered that the policy categorically suspending immigrant visas for nationals of the 75 countries be set aside. It also ordered that visa refusals based solely on the policy be vacated and returned for further consideration.

However, the decision does not automatically mean every affected Fijian applicant will receive a visa.

The court made clear that its order does not overturn refusals where applicants were found ineligible on other grounds under US immigration law.

The judgment effectively removes nationality alone as the barrier imposed by the January policy, restoring the opportunity for affected applicants to have immigrant visa applications considered under the normal statutory requirements.

item.title: ‘Motherhood penalty’
item.description: FIJIAN mothers are facing a “motherhood penalty” at work, with limited breastfeeding support and potential income losses when they take time off to care for sick children, says perinatal support group Mama Talanoa founder Mercedes Swann. Speaking during a dialogue on postpartum depression, Mrs Swann said policy changes were needed to better support women during pregnancy and after childbirth.
item.content:encoded:
FIJIAN mothers are facing a “motherhood penalty” at work, with limited breastfeeding support and potential income losses when they take time off to care for sick children, says perinatal support group Mama Talanoa founder Mercedes Swann.

Speaking during a dialogue on postpartum depression, Mrs Swann said policy changes were needed to better support women during pregnancy and after childbirth.

She called for extended maternity leave and workplace arrangements that allow mothers to breastfeed, express and safely store breast milk after returning to work.

She said mothers could also face financial pressure when they stayed home to care for sick children or during floods, cyclones and school closures.

“There really is this motherhood penalty going on where mothers are penalized at work because they are a mom for simply being a mom.”

Mrs Swann said cultural attitudes also made it difficult for women to speak openly about mental health.

“In our Fijian culture it is very much taboo to talk about mental health.

“We just have this culture of just get through it and you’ll be fine.”

She said families often focused on the newborn while overlooking the mother’s wellbeing.

“A baby was born, yes, but a mother was also born.”

She called for safe spaces and stronger support from families, communities and churches.
